data.title: Polish hillforts expedition 2 – Biskupin, Wenecja, Wyszogród and Góra Zamkowa
data.excerpt: The second day of our expedition to Poland took us to Biskupin, where an open-air archaeological museum reconstructs a Lusatian hillfort built in the winter of 738 BC together with an early medieval Slavic settlement. We went on to the ruined castle at Wenecja with its museum of siege engines, to Wyszogród on the bank of the Vistula and, after dark, to the hillfort of Góra Zamkowa in Bydgoszcz.
data.metaDescription: The second day in Poland: the Biskupin open-air museum with its Lusatian hillfort and Slavic settlement, then Wenecja, Wyszogród and Góra Zamkowa.

children.text: Biskupin
After the first day spent in Kraków and Bnin we moved in the late night hours to Biskupin, where one of the best-known Polish open-air archaeological museums and a very fine museum are located.

It is possible to stay right in the grounds of the open-air museum, where comfortable rooms are available in the so-called Dom Muzealnika. Since there is no reception there, entry was based on a numerical combination, which yielded a key only to one shared room, and only after a longer search did we find out that the keys to our rooms were hanging on a hook inside it. For a while we felt as if we were in a well-made adventure game, but perhaps that was also the work of Lukáš’s good beer, which we had been sampling a little along the way.

In the morning we waited for the museum to open and immediately set off to get to know the earliest history of Poland. The grounds of the open-air museum are notionally divided according to the various historical periods, and one has to begin chronologically in the shelters of Palaeolithic hunters and then move on through the amazing Neolithic longhouses towards the Lusatian hillfort. After passing through the hillfort you then continue into the fortified early medieval Slavic settlement.

children.text: Two Neolithic longhouses are furnished, and from their interior fittings it can be seen quite well that the houses served not only to accommodate a larger number of inhabitants, but also their animals, and at the same time as production areas and storerooms.

The hillfort at Biskupin is linked with the Lusatian culture, which inhabited extensive territories of central, northern and western Europe at the turn of the Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age. Its ethnicity has not been demonstrated so far; it is probably a matter of the Indo-European sphere, from which the later-formed European nations, among them the Slavs, also derive.

On the basis of research into the structural elements of the internal buildings and of the fortification it was established that the hillfort was most probably built in the winter of 738 BC. It arose on a marshy island in Lake Biskupin (today a peninsula), roughly oval in shape and c. 2 ha in area (c. 1.3 ha within the waterfront). The island rose 0.8–1.2 m above the waters of the surrounding lake. The Biskupin hillfort was inhabited for c. 150 years.

children.text: There were 13 longhouses in the settlement, arranged in rows along 11 streets covered with wooden paving, each 2.5 m wide. Each contained a “housing unit” with an average size of about 8 × 10 m, in each of which one family probably lived. They were separated from the other “flats” by a wooden wall. It is estimated that 800 to 1,000 people inhabited the settlement. The settlement was enclosed by a timber-and-earth rampart with an open grillage construction, 740 m long, 3 m wide and probably as much as 6 m high, with an entrance gate. The hillfort was surrounded by a breakwater 2 to 9 m wide, built of diagonally driven piles.

children.text: Two more pleasant surprises awaited us in the grounds of the open-air museum. There is a replica of the Zbruch idol here, which unfortunately we had not had the chance to see in person in Kraków. The greatest hit, however, was when we discovered the manorial court in which part of our favourite film Stará Báseň (An Ancient Tale) was shot. We had no idea about this at all and we really did savour it.
After visiting the open-air museum, a very fine museum with a great many Lusatian exhibits was still waiting for us.
Wenecja

We really did not want to leave the hillfort, but we had to keep to the timetable, so we moved on. Before that, however, we had lunch in a restaurant that lies across the road opposite the open-air museum. It is self-service, but we can only warmly recommend it. The quality-to-price ratio was excellent and I still remember, for instance, those roast potatoes.   
Not far from Biskupin, Čendo discovered the ruins of an interesting medieval fortress in the village of Wenecja. We were surprised that there is a museum of siege engines in the grounds of the castle ruins. Catapults, a trebuchet, battering rams, a siege tower and other interesting devices are reconstructed here at life size, which we saw live like this for the first time.

children.text: In the second half of the 14th century the small village of Wenecja was the centre of the estate of Mikołaj Nałęcz of Chomiąża, castellan of Nakło and judge of Kalisz, whom his contemporaries called the Venetian Devil. Mikołaj probably earned this unflattering nickname, which later appeared in many tales, because of the severity of the punishments he imposed on his serfs and because of his adventurous nature, which often provoked conflicts with his neighbours and political opponents. The castle on the edge of the village was probably built before 1390, and as early as 1395, during one of many neighbourly disputes, it was attacked and partly destroyed by troops sent by the Grzymalici in their quarrel with the Nałęcz family. After the founder’s death in 1400 the castle passed into the hands of his grandson Mikołaj Pomian of Warzymowo. At that time, between 1411 and 1420, a fire broke out in the castle which caused damage so great that the then owner decided to sell it, and in 1420 the Archbishop of Gniezno, Mikołaj Trąba, became the new owner of the fortress.

children.text: Soon after this transaction the castle was modernised. From then on it served as the main seat of the bishops and replaced the outdated manor house in Żnin. After its enlargement in 1436 it also served for a time as a prison for opponents of the church and for “disobedient” priests, especially for those who supported the Hussite movement, which was very active at that time. Despite costly investments, the further development of the fortress was soon halted by political events and administrative decisions that sealed its collapse. The end of the Thirteen Years’ War with the signing of the Second Peace of Toruń in 1466 meant that this site lost its strategic importance. The bishops too came to Wenecja less and less and finally, in view of the administrative reform of Bishop Jakub of Sienno, the decision was taken to demolish the castle. Thus in 1479–80 the castle walls were pulled down and the building material thereby obtained was used for the construction of a new masonry archiepiscopal seat in Żnin. Wenecja was thus one of the few defensive seats on the Polish lowland that ceased to function at the end of the Middle Ages.
Wyszogród
Our next stop was Wyszogród castle. We were in quite a hurry so as to make it before dark, which fortunately we managed. It lies on the edge of the city of Bydgoszcz, on the bank of the Vistula.

children.text: The castle at Wyszogród was built at the beginning of the 13th century by Duke Konrad I of Mazovia on the site of an older fortress. It was probably not a masonry structure from the outset, but originally a timber hillfort. We even came across the information that one of the Slavník family (Vojtech / Adalbert, bishop and martyr) stopped at the hillfort. In the course of the thirteenth century one of the main seats of the Mazovian dukes was located here. The masonry complex may have come into being during the reign of Casimir the Great, which, however, is not confirmed by the chronicles of Janko of Czarnków and Jan Długosz. The greatest flourishing of the castle and the settlement came in the time of dukes Siemowit III and his son Janusz I, who in 1398 granted Wyszogród a town charter. This is the most probable period of the construction of the masonry fortress.

It was probably a quadrangular foundation with a tower. The further history of the castle is not known; in the 18th century it was a ruin, which the Prussian authorities dismantled for building material in 1798. After this demolition an octagonal masonry castle tower remained until 1870. No masonry remains of the castle are visible, only massive ramparts and ditches. It stands on Castle Hill, which is easily accessible; it is about a 5-minute walk from the car park by the supermarket.
Góra Zamkowa

Our last stop was the hillfort of Góra Zamkowa in Bydgoszcz. Unfortunately already after dark, but all the more atmospheric for that and in good spirits. Zámčisko is reminiscent of many Slovak hillforts and small forts, because it lies on a hill and not in the lowlands like most other Polish hillforts. So we did a bit of walking by headlamp light and then savoured the atmosphere of the ancient fortress and the views of the illuminated night-time city around the hillfort. 
  Polish sources on the hillfort state that on a spur of the Fordon slope, which separates the Świecie upland from the Toruń Basin, there is a hillfort of the people of the Lusatian culture and of the early Middle Ages. Its summit is formed by a flat plateau with steep slopes. To the east runs a picturesque “ridge” of the plateau, which is surrounded on one side by a valley and on the other by the Brda–Vistula glacial valley.

children.text: While the first investigations of the hillfort pointed to early medieval occupation, later research brought a large quantity of pottery of the Lusatian culture from the Hallstatt period. It is thus evident that the early medieval occupation followed on from an older hillfort from the time of the Lusatian culture. During the excavations fifteen utility pits were discovered here containing pottery, a fragment of a bronze pin, a stone axe and two clay spindle whorls. The hillfort was enclosed by a timber-and-earth rampart and an all-round dry ditch linked to an additional arm of a transverse ditch placed at the point of the most favourable access to the hillfort from the upland. The construction of the rampart consisted of longitudinal beams that were fixed by transverse beams, thereby creating a grillage construction of the bank. The circuit dry ditch was made by a terrace-like cut into the natural slope of the hill with a gradient of 20–30 degrees. As a result, the inner wall of the ditch, about 5 m high, had a slope on the outside that made access to the rampart difficult. On the way down from the hillfort we played at being metal detectorists and with our wooden "machines" we thoroughly surveyed the access route to the hillfort. For our survey we used good-quality wooden detectors of the
Cenwood
brand.
